newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec City plans to erect de Gaulle statue.
newsitem.headline: Quebec City plans to erect de Gaulle statue.

text.p: Charles de Gaulle, the former French president who cheered Quebec separatists with an impassioned Montreal speech in 1967 supporting the province's independence, is returning to haunt Canadian politics.

Quebec City, the capital of the French-speaking Canadian province, plans to commemorate de Gaulle by erecting a statue of the late president near the Plains of Abraham, a peaceful grassy site overlooking the St. Lawrence River, where British troops defeated the French for control of Canada in 1759.

The C$215,000 ($159,000) project is raising the hackles of English-speaking Canadians, who have bitter memories of de Gaulle's exhortation to an ecstatic crowd from the balcony of Montreal city hall in 1967: "Vive le Quebec libre" (Long live a free Quebec).

De Gaulle's comment is credited with boosting separatist sentiments in Quebec just as Canada was celebrating its centennial, and it remains a sore point in diplomatic relations between Canada and France.
Worried Canadian officials are also looking into reports that the French government plans to issue a postage stamp commemorating de Gaulle's Montreal visit.

Quebec's separatist Parti Quebecois government and Quebec City Mayor Jean-Paul L'Allier, who supports independence for the province of 7.3 million people, offer no apologies for commissioning the statue.
"De Gaulle to us is not first and above all the man who said 'Vive le Quebec libre.' He is the man who, in the early 1960s, opened the windows of Quebec to the world," L'Allier told Reuters.

Aside from saying the 8.5-foot (2.6-metre), 705-pound (320 kg) bronze statue is an affront to the political sensibilities of some Canadians, opponents argue that it is a waste of money when the heavily indebted Quebec government is slashing spending to meet its budget deficit forecasts.
"It doesn't make any sense," Quebec City Councilman Martin Forgues said.
Plans are to unveil the statue on July 23, the 30th anniversary of de Gaulle's Montreal speech.
